# Evaluation & Trade-offs

Our evaluation ran against ten synthetic personas, each
exercising a distinct decision path through the analysis engine over a fixed
twelve-month window covering several different cases including the ordinary decisions 
(keeping a plan, acquiring one, cancelling one) plus some stress testing and edge cases. 
The comparison uses a Langfuse dataset whose items hold the raw `load_context` payload as 
input and the engine's normalized recommendations as expected output. The `baseline` is a 
single LLM call with the customer's raw data in the prompt and the `main` arm is our agentic 
pipeline. Both run against the same five scores. Since `main` returns the engine's own output, 
which also act as the ground truth, its scores follow by construction, and the experiment measures 
how a single LLM call performs against that reference. Three evaluators are deterministic
guardrails on a recommendation's shape (`plan-in-catalog`, `action-in-vocabulary`,
`savings-non-negative`), one measures agreement with the engine's decision (`category-agreement`), 
and the last is an LLM judge on numerical soundness (`recommendation-soundness`).
The baseline's structural results are flawless: it never invented a tariff, never left the action vocabulary, 
and never claimed a negative saving, scoring 1.00 on all three guardrails. Its decisions are roughly two-thirds
right, with three runs scoring `category-agreement` between 0.61 and 0.69, so on about a
third of categories it reached a different verdict from the engine.
The soundness judge passed zero of ten items in both runs, passing an item only when
every figure in it is correct. Julia Berger's case shows the pattern: the baseline
picked both correct actions, but then priced the upgrade at €1,449.37 where the engine computed
€1,619.92. The advice was correct and the item still failed, on the number.

## Token usage and cost drivers

Token counts are measured from Langfuse traces. An analysis run averages 7,845 tokens against 
the baseline's 46,619, a 5.9x difference that widens to 9.3x on input, the part that scales with 
the customer's data volume. The baseline spends 69% of its tokens re-reading raw trip legs, ours 
spends 56% on output. As Leg-level history in the prompt is the dominant cost driver, 
baseline cost rises with how much a customer travels, so the heaviest travellers, the ones with most to gain, 
are the most expensive to serve. Our analysis path stays close to flat in trip count.
With our pipeline we trade efficiency against adaptability. Every new numeric
capability must be written as engine code rather than added to a prompt, which is
slower to build and impossible to extend at conversation time. Latency and token cost
fall in return. Run sequentially over the ten personas, an analysis takes a median of
28 seconds against the baseline's 71, and the baseline's tail is far heavier, with a
slowest persona of 878 seconds against our 65.
